passage: Wasim, I'll tell you what happened, but don't laugh. Last month I got into a mess. A boy from Class Eleven kept following me home and asking for money, and I gave him some twice because I was scared. I told nobody for three weeks. Then one night I couldn't sleep and I went to Papa's room. My heart was thumping. I expected shouting, and I already had my excuse ready. Instead he sat up, listened without stopping me and said, "Thank you for telling me. Let's think about what to do." He didn't punish me for giving the money. We went to the school together next morning. I still feel nervous, but I don't feel alone. Suraj.

qa.q: How long did Suraj tell nobody?
qa.a: Suraj told nobody for three weeks.

qa.q: Why did Suraj have an excuse ready when going to Papa?
qa.a: Suraj expected shouting and punishment and felt afraid, with a thumping heart. Suraj was also ashamed of having given the money.

qa.q: What did Suraj's father do that made it easier to confide?
qa.a: Papa listened without interrupting, thanked Suraj for telling and did not punish Suraj, then went with Suraj to the school.

qa.q: How might Suraj's father have felt hearing the story?
qa.a: He may have felt worried and angry at the older boy but stayed calm, so Suraj would feel safe. 🙂

grounding: A teen confides an unsafe situation to a parent who listens first and stays calm.

passage: I'm Baljeet, the school librarian here for eleven years, and I noticed this last week. Kiran stayed behind at closing time, fidgeting with a bookmark, then went to Mrs Sandhu, the counsellor, whose room is next to mine. The door was open a crack. I heard Kiran say something about marks and about not sleeping, and then a pause, and Mrs Sandhu's voice, low and calm. She didn't say 'why did you do that'. She said, 'Tell me more.' I don't know what was said after that. But when Kiran came out, she had the look of someone who has put down something heavy, and she took a book on drawing.

qa.q: What was Kiran fidgeting with at closing time?
qa.a: Kiran was fidgeting with a bookmark.

qa.q: What might Kiran have been feeling when she stayed behind and fidgeted?
qa.a: She may have been nervous and worried about her marks and sleep, and unsure whether to speak. Baljeet doesn't know what was said after that.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do that helped Kiran open up?
qa.a: She stayed calm, didn't blame, and said 'Tell me more' to invite Kiran to keep talking.

qa.q: How might Mrs Sandhu see Kiran's visit?
qa.a: She may see it as a brave first step, and a chance to keep listening and help with the worries about marks and sleep.

grounding: A teen confides stress to a counsellor who listens calmly, seen by a librarian.

passage:
Week 1: In the lab, Suraj knocked a microscope off the bench and cracked its lens. He went to his class teacher, Irfan Sir, and told him. Irfan Sir listened first, then said calmly, "Thank you for coming straight to me. Accidents happen."
Week 4: Suraj stayed back after class. "Sir, can I talk about something? I can't sleep before exams. My chest goes tight." Irfan Sir sat down with him, didn't rush, and helped him book a chat with the school counsellor for the next day.
Week 9: An older boy from the bus stop kept offering Suraj rides home and telling him not to mention it. Suraj didn't wait this time. He told Irfan Sir that morning. Irfan Sir thanked him, informed the principal and Suraj's parents that day, and arranged the school van for him.
"Why did you tell me so fast?" Irfan Sir asked. "Because of the microscope," Suraj said.

qa.q: What did Suraj crack in Week 1?
qa.a: He cracked the lens of a microscope.

qa.q: Why did Suraj tell Irfan Sir about the rides so quickly?
qa.a: Suraj felt he could trust Irfan Sir, because the calm response to the microscope and the exam worries had made him feel safe telling him things.

qa.q: What did Irfan Sir do that made each disclosure easier?
qa.a: He listened first, stayed calm, thanked Suraj for telling, and acted without punishing, so Suraj kept coming back.

qa.q: What would change if Irfan Sir had shouted about the microscope?
qa.a: Suraj might have kept his exam stress and the unsafe rides secret, feeling that telling only brought trouble.

grounding: The three beats show a teenager confiding a mistake, stress and an unsafe situation to a teacher whose calm listening makes later disclosure more likely.

passage:
Aparna, you ask why you can tell me things you can't tell anyone else? Let me, your old Kamal Dadu, tell you where that started.
At fifteen I borrowed my father's new bicycle without asking and left it outside a cinema. It was stolen. I walked home sick with fear. In our house, mistakes meant the belt.
But that night my father just sat on the step. "Tell me everything first," he said. I did. He didn't shout. He said, "We'll go to the police station together tomorrow. And you'll walk to school for a while."
I was shocked.
Two years later, when some older boys at college pushed me to carry a packet for them and said not to ask what was in it, I went straight home and told him. He came to the college the next day.
If he had beaten me over the bicycle, I would never have told him about the packet.

qa.q: Where did Kamal leave his father's bicycle?
qa.a: He left it outside a cinema.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling walking home after the bicycle was stolen?
qa.a: He was sick with fear, expecting to be punished with the belt as usual.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Kamal Dadu's story?
qa.a: His father listening first and staying calm about the bicycle, which later made Kamal tell him straight away about the unsafe packet.

qa.q: How might Kamal's father have seen that night on the step?
qa.a: He seems to have decided that hearing the whole story mattered more than punishing, perhaps seeing how frightened his son already was.

grounding: The elder's story shows that a parent's calm listening after a mistake made the teenager confide in him later about an unsafe situation.

passage:
Aparna's father, Kunal, was zipping his suitcase for a seven o'clock flight when she came into the room, pale.
"Papa, I have to tell you something, and you have to go soon."
He glanced at the clock. Forty minutes before the taxi. He sat down on the bed anyway.
"Tell me."
"This evening I was cycling in the lane and I scraped Mehta Uncle's car. A long line. And I... rode away. Nobody saw."
She waited for the explosion.
Kunal breathed out slowly. "Thank you for telling me, even with me leaving. That took courage."
"Are you angry?"
"A bit. Mostly I'm glad you came to me. Let's go now, together."
They rang Mehta Uncle's bell. Aparna apologised herself. Mehta Uncle said they'd sort out the repair later.
Kunal made his taxi with four minutes to spare.

qa.q: What time was Kunal's flight?
qa.a: It was a seven o'clock flight.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling when she told her father?
qa.a: Aparna was pale and afraid, expecting an explosion of anger and punishment.

qa.q: What did Kunal do that encouraged honesty?
qa.a: He sat down despite the rush, listened first, thanked her for telling, admitted he was a bit angry but calm, and helped her put it right.

qa.q: How might Mehta Uncle have felt when Aparna apologised herself?
qa.a: He was probably annoyed about the scratch but touched by her honesty, which may be why he was willing to sort out the repair calmly.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager confiding a mistake to a parent who listens first and stays calm under time pressure.

passage: Kunal hovered in the kitchen doorway of their Pune flat while Kavitha stirred the dal, twisting the hem of his T-shirt. "Aai, if I tell you something, will you shout first or listen first?" Kavitha turned the flame down. "Listen first. Shouting maybe later." He almost smiled. "We didn't go to Sahil's today. We went to the quarry lake. Sahil slipped on the rocks near the edge. Someone grabbed him, he's okay. But he went under for a second." Kavitha's spoon stopped. Her face went tight, then she breathed out and pulled out a stool. "Sit. Tell me all of it." He did: who went, whose idea it was, how scared he had been. She didn't take his phone or ground him right then. She said, "I'm glad you told me tonight," and called Sahil's mother to check he was really fine. A week later, when a maths test went badly, Kunal told her at the door, before she even asked.

qa.q: Where did they go instead of Sahil's?
qa.a: They went to the quarry lake.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling as he twisted his T-shirt hem in the doorway?
qa.a: Kunal was nervous and afraid of being shouted at, and probably still shaken about Sahil going under; asking 'shout first or listen first?' shows he wanted to be heard.

qa.q: What did Kavitha do that made Kunal likely to tell her again?
qa.a: She promised to listen first, steadied her own face, sat him down to hear everything, thanked him and checked on Sahil instead of punishing on the spot.

qa.q: What was it like for Kavitha to hear about the quarry lake?
qa.a: It frightened her, as her stopped spoon and tight face show, but she chose to breathe and listen so the conversation stayed open.

grounding: It shows a teenager telling a parent about an unsafe outing, and a calm, listening response that makes the next disclosure more likely.
